title: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And we have some evidence of aberrant forms having suffered severely from extinction, for they are generally represented by extremely few species; and such species as do occur are generally very distinct from each other, which again implies extinction.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “Affinities, general, complex and radiating”. Scope: aberrant (phylogenetically isolated) genera and higher groups

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A modern phylogenetic-isolation operationalization permits a strong partial test. Fossil completeness is inadequate to establish severe extinction for all isolated groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define aberrance as high phylogenetic isolation, then test whether isolated extant clades have low extant richness, high pairwise disparity, and fossil evidence of formerly greater diversity. Joint evidence supports their interpretation as extinction relicts.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Missing fossils can make a genuinely old sparse clade appear always species-poor.

Aberrant is a historical qualitative category.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Isolation, richness and fossil diversity can be measured separately, which avoids defining aberrant groups by the very poverty being tested. Trees and occurrence databases cover living isolation well and past richness unevenly. A birth-death null is essential and is also the reason the pattern, even if found, only partly discriminates relict status from passive rarity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define phylogenetically isolated groups by long stem branches or high evolutionary distinctiveness, independently of their living species count, then test whether they have unusually few species, unusually large gaps among those species, and richer extinct membership. The claim is confirmed if isolation predicts species poverty and within-group disparity beyond a birth-death null and fossils show former richness, and refuted if isolated groups are not species-poor or show no sign of lost diversity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Calling a group aberrant because its species are very distinct, and then treating that distinctness as a result, is circular unless fossils or an independent isolation measure is used.

The fossil record of the relevant stem groups is strong for some vertebrates and poor for most aberrant invertebrates and plants.

Under ordinary speciation and extinction, long-branched groups are often species-poor by chance, so poverty is not by itself evidence of a failed group.
